title: The body is the field
hookLine: the Gita began on a battlefield; chapter thirteen says the real field is you
carry: the body is the field; you're its knower

cards: Go back to the Gita's very first line. The blind king Dhritarashtra asks: on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do? Dharmakshetre, kurukshetre.
The whole book opens on a field. Two armies, dust, chariots, a man about to break down. Twelve chapters later, chapter thirteen picks up that same word, field, kshetra, and turns it around.
The field, Krishna says, isn't only out there where the armies stand. You're standing in it. You are it.

teach.h: THIS BODY IS CALLED THE FIELD.
teach.b: Chapter thirteen opens with a definition.
This body, Arjuna, is called the field, and the one who knows it, the sages call the knower of the field. Kshetra, the field. Kshetrajna, the knower of the field.
Picture a farmer's field. Weeds and wheat grow there. Weather passes over it.
Seasons change it. And at the edge stands someone who watches it and knows it, who isn't the dirt. Hindu teachers call that knower in you the atman, the self.
Then the line that makes this chapter well-known: know me also as the knower of the field in all fields. The same knower, in every body. Hindu schools read that line differently.
Advaita teachers say the knower in you and the divine knower are finally one. Ramanuja and the Vaishnava schools say the divine dwells in every knower as its inner guide, close but not identical.
Both read it from the same verse. Then verses five and six list what's in the field, and the list is bigger than you'd guess. The elements.
The sense of I. The intellect. The senses and the mind, and what they reach for.

teach.h: EVEN DESIRE AND PAIN ARE FIELD.
teach.b: Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the body as a whole, awareness, steadiness.

Your wanting, your not wanting, even your moods: all field, things that grow and change and pass. So when anger comes up, the Gita's picture says: something is growing in the field. You can notice it from the edge.
You are not only the weather.

how: Hindu teachers often use Gita 13's field and knower of the field (kshetra and kshetrajna) in meditation and study, as a way of noticing the body and mind as something known, and asking who the knower is.

o: the field: body and mind, all that's known
the world outside, beyond the body
the soul that watches from the edge

games.q: the field and its knower — tap the pairs.
p: the Gita's first word: the field of dharma

s: in Gita 13 the field includes only the physical body
verses 5–6 add the mind, the sense of I, desire, aversion, pleasure and pain.
the Gita's very first verse names a field
dharmakshetre kurukshetre: on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus.
every Hindu school reads 'the knower in all fields' the same way
Advaita reads the knowers as finally one; Ramanuja's school reads the divine as the inner guide of each.

games.q: anger flares in you during a fight with a friend. using chapter thirteen's picture, what is the anger?
o: a sign you've failed at the practice.
games.why: something in the field. the Gita lists desire, aversion, pleasure and pain as field, known by the knower at the edge.

practice: Walk the edge of your own field: the body's weight, its warmth, the places that ache; the breath coming and going; a thought arriving, maybe a worry, maybe a wish. Field, all of it.
Then, for a moment, notice the one noticing, without naming it, and just watch things grow and pass from the edge.

wordCard.voice: Kshetra, the field. Gita thirteen: the body, with its senses, desires and moods, is the field; the one who knows it is the knower of the field, kshetrajna.

orig.note: Sanskrit: kshetra, field; the same word as in Kurukshetra, the battlefield where the Gita is spoken.

carryVoice: Your line: the body is the field; you're its knower. The same word the Gita opens with, turned inward. More of the field tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 13.1–13.2 (the field and the knower of the field; the knower in all fields)
